name: PT Darma Henwa Tbk

frontmatter.title: Darma Henwa: a real fleet turnaround, a rate-led revenue line and a copper option priced on faith
frontmatter.summary: Darma Henwa's owned fleet has lifted margins and cash generation, but revenue growth is rate-led while client volumes fall and capex has not stepped down. The shares trade well below our fundamental value; the gap rests on the GMR copper-gold appraisal. We rate the stock ADD with a Rp270 target, just below the house BUY threshold.
thesis: The in-house fleet is real. The owned batches lifted the gross margin to 20.2% in our forecast and the subcontractor line fell to IDR593.4bn in the first nine months of 2026; this is operating leverage from a completed capital programme, not a coal-price windfall [S4, S6].

Revenue is rate-led, not volume-led. KPC's own mine output fell in FY2025 and the nine-month revenue increase came from higher rates and the Arutmin extension, so we forecast growth of 8.5% then 5.0%, not a volume cycle [S3, S4].

Capex has not stepped down. Nine-month capex was flat year on year at IDR1,341.6bn and a subsidiary drew new equipment credit in October 2026; we hold FY2026E capex at 25.0% of revenue and the long-run rate above D&A [S4, S10, F52, F105].

GMR is the swing factor. The copper-gold asset is carried at audited appraised value less deferred tax, with no resource statement published; a write-back to the IDR844.5bn consideration is the quantified downside the market is trying to price [S4, S5].

The konglo lens does the regime work. Price is 0.82x our current fundamental value of Rp270; with no HSC listing, no enforcement and a compliant free float [house konglo registry, as-of 27 October 2026], the base regime closes 30% of the log discount over twelve months [S0].
We rate DEWA ADD with a Rp270 target, 23.7% total return. That is a thin margin just below the BUY threshold, and the rating is sensitive to the GMR bridge [S0].

blocks.text: DEWA is a coal-mining services contractor that spent the last two years converting itself from a subcontracted labour broker into an owner of heavy equipment. The operating evidence is in the numbers: nine-month revenue of IDR5,102.0bn came against IDR4,650.4bn a year earlier, gross profit reached IDR1,034.8bn, and the subcontractor line in cost of revenues fell to IDR593.4bn as the owned fleet took over waste removal [S4]. The company is no longer a pure pass-through of someone else's mining plan.

The growth, however, is not a volume cycle. KPC's revenue rose while its own mine output fell: overburden removal at the KPC project was 102 million bcm in FY2025 against 106 million bcm in FY2024 and coal production was 10.5 million tonnes against 11.2 million tonnes [S3, F71, F72, F74, F75]. The nine-month increase came from rates, mix and the Arutmin extension, not from more material moved, and the company does not publish quarterly physical volumes [S4]. That distinction matters for the forecast: a contractor paid per cubic metre cannot compound a rate increase the way a miner compounds a commodity price.

The market has moved the other way. DEWA shares trade at Rp220, near the bottom of their twelve-month range, after the Indonesian concentrated-ownership complex de-rated through 2026 [S0, S9]. Our current fundamental value is Rp270 and our twelve-month value is Rp312; the price is 0.82x the current value. We do not treat that gap as a reason to bend the fundamentals: the model values the contract business on its own cash flows to the end of the client licences and carries the GMR copper-gold asset at its audited appraisal net of deferred tax, then lets the konglo lens decide how much of the discount closes. That lens produces a Rp270 target and our ADD rating.

The variant view is narrow and uncomfortable. The contract business alone is worth materially less than the share price, and the rest of the equity value is GMR, an asset for which the market does not pay the independent appraisal [S5]. Market capitalisation is IDR8,590.7bn and the GMR bridge is IDR6,699.1bn less IDR1,305.8bn of deferred tax at 99.8% ownership, so the asset accounts for more than half of the equity value while the contract business trades below our DCF [S0, S5, F19, F90, F46]. The market is not marking GMR at zero, but it is not paying the appraisal either. If GMR is real, the stock is cheap; if it is not, the downside is the contract business and the debt that funds it. We keep the audited appraisal in the base because the method card forbids a default haircut on a sourced asset value, and we put the write-back in the bear case and in the risk section rather than shading the base [S5].

What moves the value: first, GMR exploration and permitting news, because it is the largest single asset in the valuation; second, the durability of the KPC and Arutmin contracts through the RKAB cut and the state-exporter transition; third, capex, which has not yet stepped down and is the reason free cash flow is thinner than the fleet story implies [S3, S4, S7]. The two things that could break the thesis are a GMR write-down and a related-party contract reset on worse terms. The rating is an ADD with little room for error: 23.7% total return sits just under the house BUY threshold, and the target is below our twelve-month value because the konglo discount only partly closes.

PT Darma Henwa Tbk is a general mining contractor listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange since 2007, providing integrated mining services: land clearing, topsoil and overburden removal, drilling and blasting, coal getting, hauling, barging, port handling and mine rehabilitation [S3, S6]. It reports two segments, mining services and other services, and the business is overwhelmingly the first: overburden removal and coal production for two coal-mining clients in Kalimantan. The company employed 5,184 people at the last count [S0].

The revenue model is rate-based, not commodity-based. DEWA is paid for material moved and coal produced and hauled, so its top line follows its clients' mine plans and the rates negotiated in the operating agreements. In FY2025 the company moved 139 million bcm of overburden and produced 17.0 million tonnes of coal [S3, F21, F22]. The trend under those totals is the important part: KPC's waste removal fell to 102 million bcm from 106 million bcm in FY2024 and 122 million bcm in FY2023, while Arutmin's rose to 36.5 million bcm from a depressed 28.0 million bcm but remained below its 54.0 million bcm level two years earlier [S3, F71, F72, F73, F77, F78, F79]. Coal output followed the same path, with KPC at 10.5 million tonnes against 11.2 million tonnes and Arutmin at 6.5 million tonnes against 6.1 million tonnes [S3, F74, F75, F80, F81]. This is a contractor whose clients were already moving less material before the national quota cut.

The fleet split is the strategic story. 95.2 million bcm of waste removal and 12.5 million tonnes of coal came from the in-house fleet in FY2025, leaving subcontractors to move 46.9 million bcm of overburden [S3, F25, F26, F83]. The public-expose deck shows material moved by the owned fleet rising while subcontracted material fell, the clearest evidence that the in-sourcing programme changed the operating model [S6]. The two batches added up to 30.0 million bcm p.a. and 25.0 million bcm p.a. of annual capacity respectively, and all heavy equipment was fully operational by the end of September 2025 [S6, F36, F37].

The client base is the defining feature of the business. In FY2025, 95.5% of revenue came from related-party customers, principally PT Kaltim Prima Coal and PT Arutmin Indonesia, both described in the financial statements as entities under common control with DEWA [S3, S5]. In the first nine months of 2026, KPC supplied IDR3,588.0bn of revenue and Arutmin IDR1,395.0bn, with third parties only IDR119.0bn; the related-party share rose to 97.7% of revenue as third-party work fell [S4, F31, F32, F33, F87]. KPC's work is the Bengalon coal-mining project in East Kalimantan plus the Lubuk Tutung coal-port operation, run through the Dire Pratama subsidiary; Arutmin's work is the Asam Asam project and its Kintap East and Kintap West extensions in South Kalimantan [S3].

The contract terms are the asset life, and they are dated. KPC's strategic, operating and schedule-services agreements were signed on 1 May 2023 for the life of the mine, with KPC's IUPK valid to 31 December 2031 [S5, F91]. Arutmin's strategic and operating agreements were extended on 19 January 2026, also for the life of the mine, with Arutmin's IUPK valid to 1 November 2030 [S5, F92]. Those two dates, not a perpetuity, are the explicit life of the contract business; the report's DCF stops in FY2031 for that reason and treats anything beyond it as renewal value.

The strategy has three legs. The first is fleet ownership and vertical integration, now largely complete. The second is cost discipline: repair and maintenance, salaries, hauling and equipment rental are the large controllable lines, while fuel is only a modest slice of cost of revenues [S4]. The third is diversification beyond coal through GMR, a copper-gold exploration project at Gayo Lues in Aceh in which DEWA acquired an indirect 99.8% stake in 2025 [S3, S5]. Management frames the next phase as a "light asset model", keeping operating capacity while being disciplined on capital expenditure through equipment and service partnerships [S3] — a claim the October equipment credit sits awkwardly beside [S10].

DEWA is a challenger, not the leader, in Indonesian mining services. The large contract miners operate bigger fleets and broader client books; DEWA's position rests on a long relationship with the KPC/Arutmin complex that dates back to the Bengalon and Asam Asam operating agreements and on the cost advantage it has just built by owning equipment [S3]. That makes the company a specialist supplier to one corporate group rather than a diversified contractor, which is both the source of its contract visibility and the source of its governance discount.

The group and controlling shareholder need careful description. The annual report's register at 31 December 2025 lists Goldwave Capital at 9.4% (quoted for Zurich Assets International), Zurich Assets International at 6.2%, PT Andhesti Tungkas Pratama at 8.5%, CIMB Securities at 6.4%, CGS International at 5.5%, the public at 63.1% and treasury stock at 0.9% [S3, S5]. There is no single line above a tenth of the capital, but the two Zurich-linked lines are an economic bloc: Goldwave is explicitly quoted for Zurich Assets, and the two together are the largest identified beneficial bloc [S3]. The company is identified as a Bakrie-group name by the Indonesian press, and its two main customers are entities under common control with it, which is how the house konglo registry classifies it [S8, S9; house konglo registry, as-of 27 October 2026]. The practical control channel is the related-party ecosystem and board interlocks, not a disclosed majority stake — a point we return to in the governance section.

Indonesian mining contractors sit between the coal miners and the equipment makers. They are paid per cubic metre moved or tonne hauled, carry the diesel, maintenance and labour risk, and are only as busy as their clients' mine plans. The business rewards fleet utilisation and cost control more than price-taking, which is why contractors with owned equipment tend to earn steadier margins than subcontracted operators.

The addressable market is Indonesian coal-mine services, and its size is set by how much overburden the coal miners must strip and how much coal they are permitted to produce. The policy lever is the government's annual RKAB production quota: the annual report records that the government cut the coal RKAB from 790 million tonnes in 2025 to 600 million tonnes in 2026 [S3, F38, F39]. A smaller national production quota does not mechanically cut contractor volumes — the mix shifts toward whichever mines keep their allocations — but it caps the growth of the whole services pool and strengthens the bargaining power of the large miners that allocate work. The evidence from DEWA's own projects is that the pool was already shrinking at the margin before the quota cut, with KPC's waste removal down over two years and Arutmin's recovery only partial [S3, F71, F72, F73, F77, F78, F79].

The second policy lever is the export channel. From 1 January 2027, coal exports must be handled by the state export vehicle PT Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia under the trade ministry regulation implementing the government regulation on strategic resource exports; existing registered-exporter permits run only to the end of 2026 [S7]. The industry association has warned that the transition could disrupt cargoes if the administrative handover is not ready [S7]. For a contractor, the direct exposure is second-order — DEWA is paid by the miner, not by the export buyer — but a disruption to client shipments feeds quickly into mine plans, payment timing and receivables.

The commodity backdrop is neutral rather than hostile. The house coal deck carries Newcastle at US$118/t and the HBA at US$112/t for FY2027E, above the long-run marker, while spot Newcastle is US$150/t (house coal deck, reviewed). The public-expose deck itself argues that price normalisation after the 2021-2022 supercycle is a more predictable planning environment for contractors, with demand still supported by Indian and Chinese power generation [S6]. We agree with the direction but not with any implication that contractor rates rise with coal prices: the rate is negotiated, and the client keeps the commodity upside.

The cost-side cycle matters more. DEWA's diesel and equipment costs are linked to oil, and the house Brent deck runs at US$96.0/bbl for FY2026E, easing to US$84.0/bbl for FY2027E against a spot of US$118/bbl (house Brent deck, reviewed). The company also flags the B50 biodiesel mandate as a cost pressure [S3]. We model fuel as a modest share of cost of revenues and pass only half of the oil move into rates in the same year, so a higher Brent path compresses the margin rather than breaking the model [S4]. The new equipment credit carries a marginal rate of 10.0% per annum, which tells us the cost of capital for fleet renewal has risen, not fallen [S10, F106].

Competitive positioning is best described through the five forces rather than a market-share table, because no reliable public share data exists for Indonesian mining services. Buyer power is very high: two related-party clients dominate revenue and can set rates and payment terms [S5, S8]. Supplier power is moderate: heavy-equipment makers have pricing power on new fleets, but DEWA has already bought its two batches and can switch to rentals or subcontractors at the margin [S6]. The threat of new entrants is moderate at the small end and low at the large-project end, where capital, safety records and client relationships are barriers. Substitutes are limited — miners can in-source or use other contractors, which is exactly the competitive pressure DEWA faces. Rivalry is intense among the large contractors, but the related-party relationship blunts it for the KPC and Arutmin work.

The moat is therefore contractual and operational rather than geological. DEWA does not own a cost-curve position in a globally traded commodity; it owns operating agreements with two mines under common control and a fleet that lowers its unit cost. The relevant "reserve life" is the contract life: Arutmin runs to its IUPK expiry on 1 November 2030 and KPC to 31 December 2031 [S5, F91, F92]. We therefore truncate the explicit DCF at FY2031 rather than assuming perpetual volumes; the terminal value after that is the value of winning a renewal, and we disclose its share of enterprise value in the valuation section.

The macro tilt the frame carries is mixed. The house macro regime is balance-of-payments pressure with a cautious stance; the commodity bloc is neutral, thermal coal is neutral, and Indonesian rate-sensitive names are on the avoid list (house macro deck, reviewed). DEWA is domestic, rupiah-earning and leveraged, so the rate-sensitive tilt is a headwind while the coal tilt is neutral. The oil-import-beneficiary avoid tilt does not apply directly, but expensive oil is a cost headwind through diesel. None of these tilts is strong enough to override the company-specific contract and asset facts [S3, S4].

Mining services is a cyclical, capital-heavy business with few structural moats. Contractors win work on safety record, fleet availability and price, and lose it when a client changes mine plan or brings work in-house. The best operators run first-quartile unit costs and keep utilisation high through the cycle; the weakest carry idle equipment and subcontract the overflow. Indonesia adds a policy layer because production quotas, export rules and royalty regimes change with each administration.

The financial history is a turnaround with one enormous accounting distortion. Revenue was IDR6,068.5bn in FY2022, IDR7,372.7bn in FY2023, IDR6,032.0bn in FY2024 and IDR6,392.8bn in FY2025, so the top line has grown only modestly while the cost base changed completely [S5]. The reported net profit of IDR4,306.7bn in FY2025 is not an operating number: it contains a non-cash negative goodwill gain of IDR4,535.4bn from the GMR acquisition, which is why the reported margin and return on equity look absurd [S5, F18]. Stripping out the non-cash other-net items, the underlying business earned a modest profit; the nine-month 2026 result of IDR513.1bn is the cleaner read on current earning power [S4, S8].

The revenue build starts from the nine-month run-rate and is deliberately decomposed by client, because that is the only decomposition the filing supports. Nine-month revenue of IDR5,102.0bn compared with IDR4,650.4bn a year earlier, but KPC supplied IDR3,588.0bn against IDR3,088.0bn and Arutmin IDR1,395.0bn against IDR1,357.9bn, while third-party revenue fell to IDR119.0bn from IDR204.4bn [S4, F28, F31, F32, F33, F70, F84, F85, F86]. KPC's revenue therefore grew despite lower own-mine output, which means the increase is a rate and scope effect, not a volume effect; the company does not disclose quarterly bcm or tonnes, so the precise split cannot be observed [S3, S4]. We carry the run-rate into FY2026E growth of 8.5%, below the nine-month pace, and then 5.0%, 4.0%, 3.5% and 3.0% as flat-to-down client volumes meet the lower national RKAB and the state-exporter transition [S3, S4, S7]. No public mine-plan volume schedule exists for FY2027E-FY2030E; we do not invent one, and we hold volumes flat with rate inflation.

The margin story is the core of the case. FY2025 gross margin was 15.1%; the first nine months of 2026 ran at IDR1,034.8bn of gross profit on IDR5,102.0bn of revenue, a realised margin of well over a fifth [S4, F28, F59]. The reason is visible in the cost lines: subcontractor cost fell to IDR593.4bn, while repair and maintenance was IDR758.3bn, salaries IDR661.0bn and fuel only IDR210.8bn [S4]. Owning the fleet converts a variable subcontractor cost into fixed depreciation and maintenance, so incremental volume drops through at a high margin. We model an effective FY2026E gross margin of 20.2% and hold the input flat in nominal terms thereafter: costs stay at the last actual in real terms, and the effective margin moves only with the oil link, not through a default wage or biodiesel squeeze [S3, S4]. On the cost base below the gross line we no longer normalise: G&A is held at the observed nine-month run-rate because the G&A note in the interim LK gives no basis to treat the salary step as non-recurring, and carrying that level rather than assuming it reverses is a value-negative change to the base that leaves the rating an ADD rather than a BUY [S4].

Depreciation is the line the data pack gets most wrong, and our restatement is deliberately conservative. IDX filings use the direct cash-flow method, so the vendor data carries a D&A charge that is a fraction of the real one; the financial statements show total FY2025 depreciation and amortisation of IDR940.7bn, of which right-of-use depreciation was IDR78.7bn [S5, F9, F10]. The company's own EBITDA bridge is IDR1,752.6bn, against operating profit of IDR726.4bn, implying a total non-cash charge above the two printed depreciation lines [S3, F88, F89]. For the first nine months of 2026 the LK prints fixed-asset depreciation of IDR826.2bn and right-of-use depreciation of IDR19.1bn, together over a sixth of revenue [S4, F110, F111]. Our FY2025A D&A line uses that combined total, giving FY2025A EBITDA of IDR1,667.1bn against the company's IDR1,752.6bn bridge; the residual gap is unprinted amortisation and other non-cash items, which we disclose rather than force into D&A. The forecast FY2026E EBITDA of IDR2,039.4bn includes the full depreciation run-rate [S3, S4, S5]. The engine flags the margin step, and the assumptions carry the observed nine-month cost mix as the justification.

Cash flow and capital allocation tell the same transition story, but they do not yet show the harvest. FY2025 free cash flow to the firm was IDR-502.6bn, negative because capex of IDR1,588.9bn absorbed the fleet build and working capital swung [S5]. By the first nine months of 2026 capex was IDR1,341.6bn, flat on the prior-year period and equal to over a quarter of nine-month revenue, while the company also spent IDR791.4bn of cash on treasury shares and paid the FY2025 dividend of IDR58.6bn [S3, S4, F15, F52, F107]. Those outflows were funded with new bank debt: bank loans rose to IDR2,268.9bn current and IDR2,306.0bn non-current at 30 September 2026, from gross debt of IDR3,559.4bn at the prior year-end, while cash fell to IDR744.9bn [S4, F34, F103, F104]. The October equipment credit of IDR149.2bn to a subsidiary, explicitly for heavy-equipment purchase, shows the capex cycle is not over [S10, F105]. We hold FY2026E capex at 25.0% of revenue and let it ease to a long-run rate above D&A so the fleet is maintained rather than run down [S4, S6, S10].

The balance sheet is more leveraged than the forecast roll implies. At 30 September 2026 the company carried current bank loans of IDR2,268.9bn and non-current bank loans of IDR2,306.0bn against cash of IDR744.9bn, so actual net debt was well above the mechanical year-end roll in the model's table, which starts from 31 December 2025 and does not carry the buyback through the cash flow [S4, F34, F103, F104]. The DCF uses the actual September net debt, not the roll. Interest cover is thin: nine-month gross profit of IDR1,034.8bn less G&A of IDR322.4bn against finance cost of IDR319.4bn is only a little over two times, and the forecast interest bill rises with the higher marginal rate we now use [S4, F60, F61, F106]. The previously described "leveraged but serviceable" balance sheet was too generous; we now call it leveraged, with a refinancing calendar that matters.

Working capital is unusual and worth watching. The FY2025 operating working capital position was negative at IDR-227.6bn, because related-party payables and receivables net close in a contractor paid by affiliated miners [S5]. By the end of September 2026, trade receivables from related parties had risen to IDR1,818.3bn from IDR1,537.2bn at the prior year-end, against nine-month revenue of IDR5,102.0bn [S4, F28, F68, F69]. That is a high receivables balance in absolute terms, but it is the mirror of the related-party model: the clients are the same corporate group, and collection is a group cash-allocation decision rather than a credit risk to an unrelated buyer. Operating cash flow of IDR1,664.8bn in the nine months was healthy enough to cover interest and part of capex, but not the buyback [S4, F108].

The forecast assumes no new net borrowing after FY2026E, with capex normalising and free cash flow covering debt service [S4]. That is the most likely path only if the fleet stays utilised and the related-party rates hold; it is not a cautious one. The bear case in the scenario section is where the volume and margin risk sits, and the GMR write-back sits outside the mechanical scenario values because the engine applies the bridge to every state of the world [S5].

Earnings-quality flags, following the house screen, are mostly optics-class rather than manipulation-class, but the capital-allocation record is poor. The accruals ratio is meaningless in FY2025 because the negative goodwill is non-cash and enormous; normalised, operating cash flow of IDR1,456.1bn was healthy against underlying profit [S5, F47]. Related-party trade receivables are large and rising, but disclosed and consistent with the client base [S4, F68]. The FY2025 result also carries non-cash write-offs of receivables, inventory and fixed assets, which we exclude from the forecast as one-offs [S5]. On the IDX regime flags, the house konglo registry (as-of 27 October 2026) records no HSC listing and no enforcement action against the company, and the annual report states that it received no exchange sanction in 2025 that would have led to a trading suspension or delisting [S3; house konglo registry, as-of 27 October 2026]. Its free float is compliant at 49.9% against the raised minimum [house konglo registry, as-of 27 October 2026], and the stock is liquid [S0]. The structure flags are real and disclosed: the 2025 debt-to-equity conversion issued new Series B shares at Rp75 to three creditors, and the 2026 buyback spent IDR950.0bn on 1,639 million shares at an average far above today's price [S3, F54, F56, F93]. We classify these as optics-class and haircut nothing in the base, but they are the reason the governance section matters.

We value DEWA with a contract-life discounted cash flow as the primary method, because the company's asset is a set of operating agreements with a finite, dated life, not a commodity reserve. The industry card's through-cycle NAV logic translates directly: the "life of asset" is the contract base, anchored on the Arutmin IUPK to 1 November 2030 and the KPC IUPK to 31 December 2031 [S5, F91, F92]. The explicit forecast therefore runs only to FY2031 and the terminal value after that is the value of renewal, not contracted volume. One timing point must be disclosed: FY2031E sits inside KPC's licence, which runs to 31 December 2031, but for Arutmin, whose IUPK expires on 1 November 2030, it is a full twelve months of assumed renewal, with FY2030E carrying the two-month November-December stub after expiry; so the final explicit year already assumes an Arutmin renewal for roughly a quarter of revenue [S5, F92]. The cost side is priced off the house Brent deck through the oil link; there is no revenue commodity price to mark to a benchmark, which is why this is a corporate FCFF model rather than a commodity-producer NAV [S0, S4]. We cross-check with EV/EBITDA and EV/Sales, the two multiples contractors are actually traded on, and we drop P/E because the FY2025 earnings base is contaminated by negative goodwill [S5].

The cost of capital is built from the house macro inputs: a rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, an Indonesia country risk premium of 2.5%, an unlevered beta of 1.00 from the industry default, relevered to 1.42 at the company's debt-to-equity ratio, a one-point size premium and a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4% [S0, S4]. The WACC keeps the house pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4%; the separate P&L interest rate is what drives the forecast interest charge — the nine-month finance charge annualised on average debt is about a tenth, and the new equipment facility carries 10.0% per annum — but it does not change the WACC's cost of debt [S4, S10, F106]. That gives a cost of equity of 16.3% and a WACC of 13.2%, with debt at 35.0% of the capital structure [S0]. The WACC is high because the name is small, leveraged and Indonesian; it is not a discretionary haircut.

The DCF produces a value of Rp241 per share, with the terminal value accounting for 69.4% of enterprise value [S0]. That is a high terminal share and we disclose it rather than bury it: in a contract-life model the terminal value is the value of renewal of the KPC and Arutmin agreements after FY2031, not a perpetuity on contracted volume [S5, F91, F92]. The explicit period captures only the documented life, except for FY2031E, which is a full twelve months of assumed Arutmin renewal, and the two-month stub in FY2030E after that licence expires, so a reader who believes neither client renews should strip the terminal value out and treat that final year as contingent; what remains is the documented cash flows plus the GMR asset [S0, S5, F92]. Enterprise value is IDR7,890.7bn [S0]. The bridge to equity adds the GMR asset at its audited acquisition fair value: net identifiable assets of IDR6,699.1bn, less the deferred tax liability of IDR1,305.8bn that the acquisition created, at 99.8% ownership [S5, F19, F90, F46]. It then subtracts net debt at 30 September 2026 — cash of IDR744.9bn against bank loans of IDR2,268.9bn current and IDR2,306.0bn non-current, plus lease liabilities — rather than a modelled roll from the December 2025 balance sheet [S4, F34, F103, F104]. That choice matters: the 2026 buyback absorbed IDR791.4bn of cash after the year-end balance sheet, and a roll that ignored it would flatter the equity value [S4, F107].

The GMR carrying value is the largest single judgement in the report. It is an independent appraiser's fair value of net identifiable assets less deferred tax, and it satisfies the method card's rule that a development asset is worth at least its sourced sunk consideration and never zero [S5, F19, F20]. There is still no published resource, reserve or feasibility study, and the subsidiary table lists the project as not yet operating [S4, F109]. An asset-value floor is not an NPV, and we say so. If the appraisal is not validated, the asset would be written back toward the IDR844.5bn consideration, removing IDR4,535.4bn of bridge value; that is the quantified GMR downside, and it sits on top of the mechanical bear case described in the scenario section [S5, F18, F20]. We do not apply a generic haircut to the audited value, because the method card bars an unsourced haircut, and we do not add a success premium, because there is no resource to support one. For a reader who marks GMR at zero, the whole company costs IDR8,590.7bn of market capitalisation plus net debt, against a DCF contract-business enterprise value of IDR7,890.7bn [S0].

The cross-checks bracket the DCF, which is the honest outcome for a contractor with a large non-operating asset [S0]. EV/EBITDA at the peer median of 10.1x gives Rp470; EV/Sales at 0.9x gives Rp190. The weights are 70% DCF, 15% EV/EBITDA and 15% EV/Sales, so the multiples together carry under a third of the value [S0]. The EBITDA leg is the least reliable. Its peer median is ABMM's multiple, a mining-services-and-coal name, while PTRO at the same screen trades far above the set on a konglo premium [S0]. The EBITDA metric is also the engine's IDR1,667.1bn, which still sits below the company's own reported EBITDA of IDR1,752.6bn because the printed depreciation lines leave some amortisation and other non-cash charge in the bridge [S3, F89]. We keep EV/EBITDA small for that reason and do not use it to set the target. The sales multiple is depressed because contractor revenue is a pass-through of client mine plans, while the peer median embeds miners' commodity revenue [S0]. The DCF, which separates contract cash flows from the GMR asset and values the contracts only over their documented life, remains the anchor, and the weighted value of Rp268 sits inside the cross-check range.

The sensitivity table shows that two assumptions dominate: terminal growth and margin for the contract business, and the GMR carrying value [S0]. A one-point change in WACC moves the DCF value by a large amount because the terminal value is discounted over the full horizon, which is why we treat the DCF as a value anchor rather than a precise price [S0]. The target is not set at the top of the sensitivity range: the konglo lens is applied after the fundamental work and pulls the target below the fundamental value, as the next paragraph explains.

What does today's price imply? The reverse DCF holds the GMR asset at its audited bridge value and solves for FY2027E revenue growth; at the current Rp220, the answer is 2.9% [S0]. That is below Indonesian nominal GDP and below CPI, so the market is pricing the contract business to shrink in real terms even with GMR carried at full audited value [S0]. The market is not marking GMR near zero — the bridge is worth more than half of the market capitalisation [S0, S5, F19, F90]. It is discounting the contractor's cash flows, which is a coherent bear view but not the most likely one given the nine-month revenue growth, the margin recovery and the in-sourcing evidence [S4].

The konglo lens is the second stage of the valuation and it is deliberately separate from the fundamental work. The engine measures the price at 0.82x our current fundamental value of Rp270 — Rp220 against that value — and keeps part of that discount for twelve months according to three regime scenarios; the same premium-kept arithmetic applied to our twelve-month value of Rp312 produces the base lens target [S0]. Because DEWA has no HSC listing, no enforcement action and a free float above the minimum [house konglo registry, as-of 27 October 2026], the base regime closes 30% of the log gap, giving a base target of Rp270; the bear regime keeps more of the discount at Rp247, and the bull regime closes more at Rp293 [S0]. The probability-weighted target is Rp270, below the fundamental value even though we rate the stock ADD [S0]. Two limits are worth stating. The lens is a deterministic function of the registry flags, not an analyst premium, and it can only move the target toward fundamental value; it cannot create value. And the GMR bridge is held at its audited value in all three regimes, because the engine applies the valuation bridge to every scenario; the GMR-specific downside and upside are therefore described in the scenario section rather than shocked through the lens [S0, S5].

The dividend is not the anchor for this name. Twelve-month DPS is Rp2, a low yield, because the company has no fixed payout policy and prioritises capex, debt service and the buyback [S3, S4]. The FY2025 profit paid IDR58.6bn of cash dividend, and the model's FY2026E payout is 16.0% of earnings, so most cash is retained for the fleet and the balance sheet [S3, S4]. The market anchor is asset value — the GMR carrying value and the contract cash flows — not dividend capacity. We state that because the industry card expects a dividend-capacity cross-check; for DEWA the cross-check does not anchor the price, and the asset-value anchor is the right one.

The business scenarios are mirrored on the same two drivers, as the method requires. The base case holds our revenue and margin path. The bear case subtracts three points of revenue growth and one and a half points of gross margin every year, as the RKAB cut binds and the state-exporter transition disrupts KPC and Arutmin cargo scheduling; the bull case adds exactly the same amounts, as the owned fleet runs at full utilisation and service rates reset with inflation [S3, S7]. The probabilities are base 50%, bear 25% and bull 25%, and the resulting targets are Rp310, Rp269 and Rp359 [S0]. The base case is the most probable path, not the cautious one: the nine-month evidence supports the revenue run-rate and the recovered margin, and the bear requires the client volume decline to resume and the in-sourcing gain to be given back in rates.

The mechanical scenarios deliberately do not shock the GMR bridge, and the reason is mechanical rather than analytical: the engine applies the valuation bridge to every scenario, and only assumptions, drivers and deck lines can be shocked. We therefore do not claim the scenario table captures GMR risk. We quantify it here instead. GMR is IDR6,699.1bn of net identifiable assets less IDR1,305.8bn of deferred tax at 99.8% ownership, and it is still not operating [S4, S5, F19, F90, F46, F109]. A write-back to the IDR844.5bn consideration would remove IDR4,535.4bn of value; applied to the bear case, that takes the value below the current share price of Rp220, which is the honest downside case and the reason the rating is fragile [S5, F18, F20, S0]. The mirror image is not in the bull case either: a resource statement that validates the appraisal is upside of the same order, and it is not in the mechanical bull value. This is the one place where the mirrored-shock requirement is not met inside the engine, and we state it rather than hide it [S0].

The konglo regime scenarios are separate and independent of the business scenarios. The lens's bear regime keeps more of the discount and targets Rp247; its base targets Rp270; its bull targets Rp293 [S0]. The reason to keep them separate is that a business disappointment and a regime shift are different events: the first changes the fundamental value, the second changes how much of the discount to that value the market closes. A reader should not add the two bear cases together as if they were one scenario.

The downside risks, ranked by likelihood times impact, are these. Related-party contract risk is high impact and medium likelihood: the clients supplied 97.7% of nine-month revenue, so a rate reset or a change in KPC or Arutmin mine plans would hit revenue directly, and there is no arm's-length market to appeal to [S4, S5, F87]. Refinancing and liquidity risk is high impact and medium likelihood: bank loans of IDR2,268.9bn current and IDR2,306.0bn non-current stand against cash of IDR744.9bn, nine-month gross profit less G&A against finance cost covers interest only a little over two times, and the newest facility is priced at 10.0% [S4, F34, F59, F60, F61, F103, F104, F106]. A refinancing at a higher rate, or a covenant test on the treasury stock, would hit equity directly. Regulatory risk is high impact and medium likelihood: the RKAB cut to 600 million tonnes and the 1 January 2027 DSI export single window are dated and real, and the industry association has already warned of cargo disruption [S3, S7]. GMR execution risk is high impact with unquantifiable likelihood: there is no resource, reserve or feasibility statement, so the carrying value could be written down or re-rated on any exploration result [S5, F109]. Commodity and cost risk is medium impact and medium likelihood: higher Brent and the B50 mandate raise diesel and maintenance costs, partly offset by pass-through [S3, S4]. Operational risk is medium impact and medium likelihood: weather, fleet availability and safety incidents affect volumes and costs, as the 2025 wet-season delays showed [S6]. Capital-allocation risk is medium impact and already realised: the buyback spent IDR950.0bn on 1,639 million shares at prices well above today's price, and the treasury stock is carried at IDR951.7bn [S3, S4, F54, F67, F93]. We found no disclosure that the treasury shares are pledged to lenders and withdraw the earlier statement that they are; if a pledge exists outside the reviewed filings, the market value of the repurchased shares at Rp220 is far below the carrying value, so coverage would be weak [S3, S4, S0, F54, F67]. Governance and regime risk is high impact and low likelihood in the base case: no HSC listing or enforcement today, but the 2026 regime has shown how fast the market can reprice concentrated-ownership names [house konglo registry, as-of 27 October 2026].

The strongest case against us is simple: more than half of the fundamental equity value is an exploration asset valued by appraisal rather than by a mine plan, inside a related-party contractor whose customers are its controlling group. If a reader marks GMR at its consideration, the fundamental value falls toward the current price and the ADD disappears, as the quantification above shows. We accept that framing rather than argue it away, and we keep the audited value in the base only because the method card forbids an unsourced haircut on a sourced asset value [S5]. The ADD is therefore GMR-validated, not fleet-only, and 23.7% of total return is a thin margin under the BUY threshold [S0].

The signposts that would change our view: a GMR resource statement or feasibility study; a KPC or Arutmin contract amendment on worse rates, or an early signal on renewal ahead of the Arutmin IUPK expiry on 1 November 2030 or the KPC IUPK expiry on 31 December 2031; a quarterly volume decline that breaks the in-sourcing margin; sustained capex above the 25.0% FY2026E rate without matching revenue; a refinancing at a higher rate or a fall in interest cover; and any HSC or enforcement action that changes the konglo regime flags [S0, S3, S4, S5, F91, F92]. Conversely, GMR exploration success, a new non-related-party contract, or an acceleration of the konglo re-rating would move us toward the bull case.

DEWA is a Bakrie-group name in the house konglo registry (as-of 27 October 2026), and the ownership map is more complicated than the old report said. The 31 December 2025 register lists Goldwave Capital at 9.4% (quoted for Zurich Assets), Zurich Assets International at 6.2%, PT Andhesti Tungkas Pratama at 8.5%, CIMB Securities at 6.4%, CGS International at 5.5%, public shareholders at 63.1% and treasury stock at 0.9% [S3, F96, F97, F98, F99, F100, F101, F102]. The FY2025 financial statements list the same register lines at 9.4% for Goldwave, 6.2% for Zurich, 8.6% for ATP, 6.4% for CIMB and 5.5% for CGS [S5], while the annual report's shareholder presentation puts the public at 63.1% [S3]. Goldwave and Zurich are linked in the register's own annotation, so they form a bloc. We withdraw the earlier statement that no holder sits above ten percent: the two Zurich-linked lines together clear that level even though no single line does [S3, F96, F97]. The market data puts insider ownership at 44.4% and the free float at 49.9% [S0]. The house konglo registry (as-of 27 October 2026) records a free float of 49.9%, comfortably above the raised minimum, so DEWA is not caught by the free-float deadlines that pressure other konglo names; the registry records no HSC listing and no enforcement action against the company.

The conversion history explains why the register and the cap table differ. The February 2025 private placement issued 18,834 million shares in total — 10,093 million shares to PT Madhani Talatah Nusantara and smaller blocks to ATP and AMM — 46.3% of the post-issue capital at Rp75, and the filings call the recipients creditors, not related contractors [S3, S6, F55, F56, F94, F95]. The 31 December 2025 register shows no MTN line and no AMM line, while ATP appears at 8.5% [S3, F98]. The most likely reading is that MTN's block sits inside the public bucket, which is 63.1% and comprises holders each below the disclosure threshold, or that it was sold; the filings do not identify the transferee [S3, F101]. We cannot close that reconciliation from the reviewed sources, so we state the gap rather than assume an owner. The beneficial owners behind CIMB Securities and CGS International are also not disclosed; both names appear only after the conversion and are broker-custody lines, not proven controllers [S3, F99, F100]. We also withdraw the label "related contractors" for MTN, ATP and AMM, because the public-expose deck calls them creditors and no reviewed source establishes a related-party link [S6].

The controller question is better answered by the related-party map than by the register alone. KPC and Arutmin are entities under common control with DEWA, and they supply almost all of the revenue [S3, S5]. The President Commissioner of DEWA is also President Commissioner of KPC and Arutmin and a director of Bumi Resources, which makes the board interlock explicit [S3]. That is the governance discount in one sentence: the customers, the controlling group and the board are the same ecosystem, and minority shareholders are price-takers on the terms of that ecosystem.

Related-party gravity is therefore extreme. Revenue from related parties was 97.7% of the total in the first nine months of 2026, and 95.5% of FY2025 revenue came from three related-party customers [S4, S3, F87, F27]. In the nine months KPC and Arutmin supplied IDR3,588.0bn and IDR1,395.0bn respectively against third-party revenue of IDR119.0bn [S4, F31, F32, F33]. Trade receivables from related parties were IDR1,818.3bn at the end of September 2026 [S4, F68]. The GMR acquisition itself was an affiliate transaction: DEWA acquired 99.8% of GMR through the realisation of an advance for investment of IDR844.5bn, with the resulting negative goodwill of IDR4,535.4bn booked to profit [S5, F18, F20, F46]. These are disclosed, but they mean the earnings quality screen's related-party test is failed by construction; the only mitigant is that the transactions are audited and the counterparties sit inside the same group economics.

On the structural flags, the 2025 debt-to-equity conversion issued new Series B shares at an exercise price of Rp75, converting debt owed to creditors into equity and cutting leverage [S3, S6]. The 2026 buyback spent IDR950.0bn on 1,639 million shares at an average price well above today's Rp220, and left treasury stock carried at IDR951.7bn [S3, S4, F54, F67, F93]. That was a large transfer from continuing shareholders to selling holders, and it used cash the balance sheet needed for the refinancing; we treat it as a capital-allocation failure, not a neutral share-count reduction. We could not find disclosure that the treasury shares are pledged to lenders, and we withdraw the earlier statement that they are [S3, S4]. If a pledge exists outside the reviewed filings, the carrying value is far above the shares' market value, so any pledge coverage would be weak [S0, F54, F67]. The asset-security package over more than half of net assets was approved at a shareholders' meeting in 2025 [S6]. We treat these as structure flags, not manipulation flags.

Audit and disclosure are adequate. The FY2025 financial statements were audited by PKF Hadiwinata, which replaced the previous auditor RSM AAJ for the 2025 financial year, and the opinion was unmodified [S3]. The auditor provided no other services according to the annual report, and the audit committee and internal audit functions are described in the governance section [S3]. The auditor change is a governance item to monitor, but the opinion and the absence of non-audit services are reassuring.

The dividend record is thin and discretionary. There is no fixed payout policy; the AGM decides, and the FY2025 profit paid a cash dividend of IDR58.6bn, a small fraction of reported profit and of underlying profit [S3, S4]. The company is prioritising capex, debt service and the buyback, which is defensible for a contractor in a fleet-build phase but gives income investors little to anchor on.

ESG exposures are those of a coal-services contractor. The company is exposed to the energy transition through its client base, to rehabilitation and mine-closure obligations, and to the social licence of its operations in Kalimantan and Aceh. It holds ISO quality, environmental and occupational-health certifications and reports zero-accident awards at the Bengalon and Asam Asam projects, which is a positive safety signal [S6]. The GMR copper-gold project adds a new ESG dimension — exploration in Aceh, permitting and community relations — that is not yet developed enough to assess [S5]. We do not apply an ESG discount to the valuation; we note it as a monitoring item.

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter. The nearest hard data point is the full-year 2026 result in the first quarter of 2027, which will show whether the nine-month margin held through the fourth quarter; the nine-month result is already filed [S4]. The 1 January 2027 state-exporter transition is the next regulatory event, and the industry association's warning means the market will watch the first cargoes through PT DSI closely [S7]. The free-float deadline of 31 March 2027 and the MSCI consultation decision by 30 June 2027 are regime events for the konglo complex rather than company-specific ones, but they set the backdrop for how fast DEWA's discount can close [house konglo registry, as-of 27 October 2026]. The contract catalysts are dated and long: the Arutmin IUPK runs to 1 November 2030 and the KPC IUPK to 31 December 2031, which is the point at which the terminal value becomes a renewal question rather than an assumption [S5, F91, F92].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are: overburden removal and coal production volumes, and the in-house versus subcontractor split; gross margin and the subcontractor, repair and fuel lines in cost of revenues; related-party receivables and collection days; gross debt, cash, the refinancing calendar and interest cover; capex against the 25.0% FY2026E run-rate; the treasury-share carrying value and any buyback restart; and any GMR exploration disclosure [S0, S3, S4, S5]. We also watch the konglo regime signals: HSC status, free-float compliance, index deletions and enforcement actions [house konglo registry, as-of 27 October 2026]. A change in any of these would trigger an update or a revision rather than a silent drift.

For Indonesian contractors, the most reliable early warning of a margin problem is not the reported gross margin but the subcontractor share of material moved: when a contractor leans back on subcontractors, the variable cost rises before the margin line shows it. The second is receivables from affiliated clients, which can lengthen without a credit event because the group allocates cash centrally. Both are worth tracking quarterly.

bear.narrative: The client-volume decline of 2024-25 continues (KPC overburden 122.09 to 102.16 million bcm and coal 9.69 to 10.51 Mt; Arutmin coal 7.46 to 6.53 Mt [F71, F73, F74, F76, F80, F82, S3]), the RKAB cut to about 600 Mt binds harder and the 1 January 2027 PT DSI export handover disrupts KPC and Arutmin cargo scheduling, so revenue growth runs three points below base and gross margin 1.5 points lower as the subcontractor mix is rebuilt. The GMR bridge is applied to every engine scenario; in this state of the world the appraisal is not validated and the asset is written back toward its Rp844.5bn consideration [F20, S5], which is a further downside not captured in the mechanical bear value.

bull.narrative: The mirror of the bear on the same drivers: client volumes stabilise as KPC and Arutmin keep their allocations through the RKAB cut, the Arutmin extension wins new Kintap scope, revenue growth runs three points above base and service rates reset with fuel and wage inflation so gross margin holds 1.5 points higher. A GMR resource statement that validates the Rp5,380bn bridge would be a further upside of the same order as the bear's write-down and is not included in the mechanical bull value.
